items_missed: No 'sound good?' confirmation. The agenda itself was good — 'We'll just start with a few questions to get us on the right track and that should just take about five to ten minutes and then we'll be able to build you an accurate quote for that' — roadmap plus timeframe, which most reps skip entirely. But she never closed it with a confirmation ask, so the differentiator flag does not count. Adding four words to a sentence she is already saying converts this from a miss to a hit.
Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up before moving into data collection.

Special considerations never probed — no question about narrow hallways, tight turns, or doorway clearance. The entire job is carrying fifteen oversized pieces through a 3,000 sq ft house to the garage, and the customer described them as 'mostly just awkward. Requires two people to carry.' Awkward-and-two-person is the definition of a tight-turn risk and it was never sized.

Packing services never offered. She asked 'No boxes,' got 'No boxes,' and stopped there. She never asked whether the china cabinet, the two bookcases, the IKEA bookcase, or the sideboard need to be emptied before move day — which is both a services question and the single biggest time variable on this job.

Access concerns never asked. No question about driveway, parking, garage door clearance, or where the truck stages. On an in-home move the truck barely matters, but where the crew parks and stages the garage does.

Disassembly / reassembly never mentioned, on a job with a dining room table, a china cabinet, and three bookcases. The customer never learned that taking legs off the table and shelves out of the bookcases is included.

The 'no hidden fees' line was said but not pitched. 'We don't have any hidden fees, just so you know' is one clause inside a 200-word run-on. The explicit list — no credit card fees, no transportation fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees — never came, and it was the differentiator most likely to land with a customer who was already balking at the minimum.

No 15-minute proration mentioned. She said the clock starts on-site and that there is a 2.5 hour minimum, then stopped. The customer's immediate objection was 'That's way more than I need' — the fact that time past the minimum bills in fifteen-minute increments is precisely the reassurance that objection needed, and it was never given.

No sense-check anywhere. The pricing, clock, insurance, and no-deposit content all came out as one continuous block. The customer's only inputs across the entire stretch were 'Sure, sure,' 'Oh, okay,' and 'That's way more than I need.'

No estimate was ever given. She collected a full inventory — fifteen pieces, itemized, with weights — and then never told the customer how long she thought it would take or what he would actually pay. She quoted the rate ($208/hr) and the minimum (2.5 hrs) and left him to do the arithmetic. The customer had already offered his own estimate — 'If you got two you strong guys that's gonna take about 15-20 minutes to get it done' — and it went uncorrected and unanchored.
No typical time range for a job of this type, no total, no equivalents. There is nothing on this call the customer could repeat back to a spouse as a number.
Walk distance never asked, on a job that is entirely carry distance — bedrooms and living room to garage in a 3,000 sq ft single-story home.

The 'that's way more than I need' objection was answered with an upsell, not the prep speech. Her response was 'you may want to utilize them even more than, you know, other things around the house, that you want moved or things from room to room.' That is asking him to buy more time, not showing him how to use the time he has to buy. The consolidation half of Save Your Ass applies directly here — emptying the china cabinet, the bookcases, and the sideboard before the crew arrives is the difference between a 2.5-hour job and a four-hour one — and it was never said.

Zero booking attempt on a call where she had already confirmed availability for the requested date. She opened with 'Great, I do have availability for that day' and closed with 'if you do change your mind and want to get on our schedule and give us a callback.' The date was open, the customer was qualified, and the ask was never made.

No BOLDED-details framing and no 'reply with any corrections' on the email handoff. She promised the email three times but never told him to verify anything in it, so the email_handoff differentiator does not count.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' and no hours or how-to-reach-us — 'give us a callback or just send us an email' was the whole close.

Customer's name used twice ('how did you hear about us, Sean?' and 'Thanks Sean have a good rest of your weekend') — one short of the 3+ standard on a call where she had his name inside the first ninety seconds.
top_strength: Bri's intake discipline is the best thing on this call and it is genuinely well built. Inside the first two minutes she had the date, confirmed availability, first name with spelling verified ('Is that S-H-U-N or WN?'), last name spelled back, phone number confirmed against what was on screen, email, and lead source — and she framed the email capture as a service rather than a data grab: 'no need to take notes, I can send all of this information over via email. Is there a good email for you?' That is a complete lead record built before a single pricing word was spoken, and it is exactly what the lowest-scoring calls in this sample are missing. Her inventory work was also patient and correct. She did not accept 'some furniture' — she opened it up with 'What else would we be moving?', let the customer go get his actual list, and then kept the door open when he remembered more ('Oh, and a ti couch from the back porch'). She caught the one real risk item unprompted: on the china cabinet she asked 'Does that one have glass in it?' before moving on. And her pricing opener was verbatim on-script — 'just, so you know, our pricing is super simple, we just charge a hourly rate' — with a solid inclusions list right behind it: 'their Dolly's wraps, pads anything that they need to protect the items... the routes, pads, gas truck to you, taxes and insurance, we don't have any hidden fees.' She also volunteered two things nobody asked her for: no deposits to get on the schedule, and a shopping tip that positioned Einstein without knocking anyone — 'I don't know if these things are important to you. But just making sure when you are shopping around making sure that they have insurance to cover the items. We have a $2,000 insurance that covers up to like during the move repair, replace or reimburse for any accidental damages.' Teaching a customer how to compare is a strong, low-pressure differentiator move.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: Bri built a complete lead record, a complete inventory, and a correct rate — and then never gave the customer a number or asked for the business. The whole call turns on one moment. He said 'That's way more than I need,' and the answer she gave was to suggest he find more work for the crew. The answer this call needed was the estimate she never delivered: 'Sean, fifteen pieces that size with two guys is going to run right at the two-and-a-half hour minimum — that's $520 all in, and if we finish early you still pay the minimum, but anything past it only bills in fifteen-minute increments, so there's no surprise on the back end. Wednesday the 16th is open right now, there's no deposit and no cancellation fee — want me to lock it in?' That single paragraph delivers the estimate, the proration, the minimum-as-floor reframe, the no-deposit differentiator, and the booking ask, and every piece of it was already sitting in her notes. Estimate-accuracy flag: no estimate was given at all on this call. That is a different failure than padding, and for the bottom-4 review it is arguably worse — a padded quote at least produces a number to measure an actual against, but this call produces nothing. The customer walked away with his own guess ('about 15-20 minutes') sitting uncorrected next to a 2.5-hour minimum, which is the exact gap that turns into a move-day argument. Every quoting call needs a stated hour range and a stated total before the close, even when the answer is 'the minimum covers it.' Second priority: the pricing block ran roughly 200 words with no breath in it — rate, truck, inclusions, hidden fees, clock start, and minimum all in one sentence, and the customer's only response across the whole thing was 'Sure, sure. Oh, okay.' Break it into three pieces with a 'does that make sense?' after each. That would also have caught his objection while she still had room to answer it, instead of after the block had closed. Third: the two missing differentiators are both free on this call. Meet Your Mover costs one sentence and matters more than usual here, because the crew is walking through his whole house and touching a 100-pound vintage cabinet he clearly cares about. On-Time Guarantee costs one sentence and he named a specific Wednesday. Finally, fix the naming on the coverage — 'a $2,000 insurance' should be 'our No Worries Damage Coverage, up to $2,000 per move' and should be paired with the 60-cents-per-pound industry baseline, because without that comparison the number sounds small rather than generous.
phone_presence_notes: Naturally warm and quick on her feet — the spelling exchange landed as a real moment ('Is that S-H-U-N or WN?' / 'UN good guess'), she reacted to his inventory with 'Okay, I love that' rather than just logging it, and she asked how he heard about Einstein and engaged the answer; held back from a 5 by using his name only twice and by a long unbroken pricing block that reduced the customer to 'Sure, sure.'
audio_review_reason: The last ninety seconds are unreadable from text. The customer's turns arrive stacked and fragmentary — 'That.' / 'Yeah, I'm not.' / 'Okay, that'd be good, that'd be good.' / 'Okay. Alright, well, okay.' — interleaved against a continuous 200-word block from Bri, so it is impossible to tell from the transcript whether he was declining while she was still talking or agreeing to receive the email. That distinction determines whether this was a lost booking attempt or a customer who was talked past, and it is the central coaching question on the call.
